newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - prices seen linked to barometer.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - prices seen linked to barometer.

text.p: U.S. domestic crude prices are expected to be tied to the barometer this week, with Monday's sharp rise linked to forecasts of an Arctic freeze extending from the Midwest to the south and eastern parts of the country.

Domestic grade differentials were steady and tracked higher with the outright price, which pulled benchmark West Texas Intermediate/Cushing up around 70 cents to $25.20 a barrel by mid-morning. That cut further into the $2.50 loss seen at the start of last week, bringing WTI within 40 cents of its December 6 high, prior to last week's resumption of Iraqi crude oil exports.
"The weather is the main thing driving this market," said a Connecticut-based trader at a major commodity house.

After many delays since negotiations began last February, Iraqi crude exports resumed over the weekend, with Turkey's TUPRAS taking the first load out of an allowed $2 billion of exports over six months under a U.N. humanitarian deal. Other exports, including those contracted by U.S. oil companies Coastal Corp and Bay Oil USA, are being loaded.
"All the bearish news, with Iraq and so on, is out there. Over the next two months the weather (in the U.S.) is going to be the main story," predicted a Houston oil broker.
Also keying market activity is the pre-holiday push to get business cleared off desks before the break.
"There are a lot of people with a lot to do this week and we are doing our homework," said a trader at a major oil company in Houston.

Weather Services Corp in Washington DC and other forecasters were calling for below-normal temperatures extending from the Midwest deep into the south -- possibly affecting Gulf of Mexico operations if it lasts long enough -- and into the high heating oil-demand area of the northeast.
However, industry experts say that it remains to be seen whether the effect on demand will be sustainable and significant.

"Cumulative degree days are what count and if we have a sustained period that is, say, five percent below normal, then that is statistically significant and would have an impact on inventories and prices...I think we are not there yet," said Theodore Eck, chief economist at oil major Amoco Corp.
He also notes that the first 15 days of this month have been above normal on a cumulative temperature basis, particularly in the key northeastern market.
"The market is going to be very sensitive to these numbers until we get a track record on this weather," said Eck.
Crude prices will be engined by the products sectors while the weather is the main factor in the frame, though if that fades soon then other influences should start to be felt, traders said.

North Sea crudes were cheapening further at the start of this week, with dated Brent sold at a 20 cent discount to January after trading flat last week. Though WTI/Brent was steady at just under $1.20 for January, a fairly sloppy North Sea market into the start of January is expected to help start eroding the premium sweet crudes have enjoyed over sour.
"I think we've hit the bottom and it'll start to head back to $1 over the next few weeks," said a Houston trader, referring to the bellwether sweet/sour differential of WTI/Cushing/WTS/Midland.
Sour has been losing ground compared with sweet all year long and has been trading between $1.50 and $1.75 for the last two months, compared with a more typical range of 75 cents to $1.50.

On the cold weather play, some traders see the rise in backwardation as overdone. "If it's the weather that's going to drive the market then I'd much rather sell January and buy February, or better still sell January and buy March," said a crude trader.
WTI January/February backwardation has climbed about 12 cents since bottoming out last week and was at around 55 cents in early afternoon, while January/March has risen to $1.08 from about 94 cents.
